I am a Ph.D. Candidate in Economics at Yale University.

I study international trade, technology, and firms, focusing on how production knowledge and new technologies spread across firms and labor markets. My work combines micro data and causal evidence with quantitative models.

My CV is available [here](cv.pdf). Email: [sabrina.peng\@yale.edu](mailto:sabrina.peng@yale.edu).

## Research

Offshoring and Knowledge Spillovers (Job Market Paper)

Workforce Age Structure and Frontier Technology Adoption: Evidence from Newly Released Software (with Tra Nguyen)

<details>
<summary>Abstract</summary>
<p>This paper provides causal evidence that aging slows technology adoption and sheds light on why. Using Lightcast job postings, we track local adoption of 15 software technologies following their releases, instrumenting local age composition with a Bartik-style measure based on historical age structure and national survival rates. Employers in older labor markets post increasingly fewer vacancies requiring the newest software: at year 4, a one-standard-deviation increase in the older-worker share reduces new-technology postings by about 15% of pre-release legacy postings share. The gap is also larger for more difficult technologies, which we measure using new LLM-based difficulty indices. We then develop a model to separate three potential channels through which aging affects technology adoption: shorter work horizon, legacy technology experience loss, and reduced learning efficiency. Removing experience loss reduces the age adoption gap by about 88%, more than removing differences in horizons or learning efficiency. The model also shows that policies affecting workforce age structure have different implications for adoption. Relative to replacement-level fertility with retirement at 70, and assuming zero net migration, a total fertility rate of 1.6 lowers aggregate adoption by 7.5%, whereas raising the retirement age to 75 has almost no effect.</p>
</details>
